matched_finding.subcategory: inadequate minimum sample size for replication goals
matched_finding.description: The minimum sample size was set at 120, yet two replications (Gordon: N=80, BYU-Sp16: N=90) fall below this threshold. The authors state 'All studies in this meta-analysis received this approval by the CREP team, collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study),' which is directly contradicted by the data in Table 1. This raises questions about inclusion criteria consistency.

matched_finding.subcategory: no reporting of participant exclusions within studies
matched_finding.description: The authors do not report whether any participants were excluded from individual replication studies (e.g., for failing attention checks, not being Facebook users, incomplete responses). Given that the measure specifically asks about Facebook perceptions, participants who do not use Facebook would provide meaningless data. No information is provided about Facebook usage rates in the samples or exclusion of non-users.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Mechanism measurement caveat removed — must distinguish pattern consistency from mechanism testing
ground_truth.original_snippet: However, the CREP studies did not include a measure of FTF vs. online anxiety, making this an interesting direction for future research.
ground_truth.description: Deleted caveat that anxiety mechanism was not measured — paper now overclaims support for social compensation theory when it only found a consistent pattern, not the proposed mechanism

matched_finding.description: The authors claim the results 'provide some support for social compensation theory' based on findings that low self-esteem individuals perceive Facebook as safer for self-disclosure. However, social compensation theory (McKenna & Bargh, 2000) specifically predicts that socially anxious or lonely individuals will use online interactions to compensate for deficits in FTF relationships, leading to actual behavioral outcomes. The present study only measures perceptions of Facebook, not actual compensatory behavior or outcomes, making the theoretical claim an overclaim.
matched_finding.quote: The present research also provides some support for social compensation theory (McKenna & Bargh, 2000; Wilson et al., 2012). This theory suggests that for those with lower self-esteem, the anxiety provoked by FTF interactions can be somewhat mitigated in online interactions.

ground_truth.original_snippet: We chose to use the restricted maximum likelihood (REML) model because it has been shown to exhibit less bias than the more commonly used DerSimonian and Laird (DL) model with small numbers of studies (Veroniki et al., 2016).
ground_truth.modified_snippet: We compared restricted maximum likelihood (REML) and DerSimonian and Laird (DL) models and selected REML as it produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates for our data (Veroniki et al., 2016).
ground_truth.description: Changed principled REML selection (less bias with small k) to post-hoc model selection based on 'more interpretable' results — explicit analytic flexibility

matched_finding.description: The authors report comparing REML and DerSimonian-Laird models and selecting REML because 'it produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates.' This post-hoc model selection based on output interpretability rather than a priori theoretical or statistical justification represents an undisclosed researcher degree of freedom. It is unclear whether this choice was pre-registered or made after examining the data.
matched_finding.quote: We compared restricted maximum likelihood (REML) and DerSimonian and Laird (DL) models and selected REML as it produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates for our data

matched_finding.subcategory: missing information on missing data handling
matched_finding.description: The authors acknowledge that 'not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc.' but do not report what was done to address this in the meta-analysis. The impact of potentially different missing data handling procedures across studies on the meta-analytic results is unaddressed.
